newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Abkhaz leader warns of war if Russian troops leave.
newsitem.headline: Abkhaz leader warns of war if Russian troops leave.

text.p: The leader of Abkhazia, which fought its way to de facto independence from Georgia in 1993, warned on Sunday of a risk of new fighting if Russia withdrew its peacekeeping troops from the former Soviet republic.

Arriving in Moscow for talks with Russian officials, Vladislav Ardzinba told Interfax news agency: "After a withdrawal of the Russian peacekeepers, the sequence of events could lead to a renewal of the conflict."

The Georgian government, which refuses to recognise the Black Sea province's claims to sovereignty, is pressing Russia to either step up the activity of its 2,500 peacekeepers in a buffer zone around Abkhazia or pull them out at the end of their present mandate on August 1.

The tone of exchanges between Moscow and Tbilisi has sharpened in recent days with officials on each side accusing the other of "blackmail" and warning that creating a power vacuum in the buffer zone could spark new fighting.
The Russian peacekeepers have been the targets of attacks, including a mine blast last week that killed an officer and wounded two other servicemen.
Ardzinba told NTV television: "The peacekeepers should stay in the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict zone just as long as is necessary for the peace process."
He said a peaceful settlement with Tbilisi was possible and called on the Georgian government to make constructive proposals.
Both sides insist they would not open hostilities.
Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze, the former Soviet foreign minister, has warned the Abkhaz it would be "suicide" for them to take on Tbilisi's rebuilt armed forces.
Last month he offered to reopen stalled peace talks but ruled out Arzinba's calls for a deal similar to the one Russia gave Chechnya recently.
The inter-parliamentary assembly of former Soviet republics grouped in the Commonwealth of Independent States issued a call for renewed negotiations on a settlement.
Meeting in St Petersburg on Sunday, delegates voiced worries over the lack of progress following the 1992-93 war that left an estimated 10,000 dead and many more homeless refugees.
